proofs.proof_tex:
We construct the priors directly for the fixed point \(x_0\) and the fixed sample size \(n\).  Let \(D=[0,1]^d\), let \(p=3/8\), and choose a nonnegative \(C^\infty\) function \(k:\mathbb R^d\to[0,1]\), supported on \([-1,1]^d\), with \(k(0)=1\).  For example, one may normalize the coordinatewise product of \(e^{-1/(1-t^2)}\mathbf 1\{|t|<1\}\).  Put
\[
 k_{x_0,h}(x)=k\!\left(\frac{\sigma\odot(x-x_0)}{h}\right),
 \qquad K_{x_0,h}(x)=k_{x_0,h}(x)^2,                              \tag{19}
\]
where \(\sigma_k=1\) if \(x_{0k}\le 1/2\) and \(\sigma_k=-1\) otherwise.  Symmetry of the support makes the sign immaterial to its size, but the orientation identifies an inward face at a boundary point.  The restriction of (19) to \(D\) is smooth, equals one at \(x_0\), and has active volume at most \((2h)^d\); truncation by the boundary can only decrease that volume.  Thus no extension of the design support is made.

At a scale \(\ell\), define
\[
 J_\ell=\{j\in\mathbb Z^d:\operatorname{dist}_\infty(\ell j,D)\le\ell\},
 \qquad
 \phi_j(x)=\prod_{k=1}^d e^{-1/(1-(x_k/\ell-j_k)^2)}
                    \mathbf 1\{|x_k/\ell-j_k|<1\},
\]
and
\[
 A_\ell(x)=\sum_{j\in J_\ell}\phi_j(x)^2,
 \qquad \psi_j(x)=\phi_j(x)A_\ell(x)^{-1/2}.
\]
The set \(J_\ell\) is finite.  For each \(x\in D\), coordinatewise nearest-integer rounding supplies \(j\in J_\ell\) for which \(\lVert x/\ell-j\rVert_\infty\le1/2\).  Hence \(A_\ell\) is bounded below on a neighborhood of \(D\) by a positive constant depending only on \(d\).  The quotient rule and rescaling consequently give, for every multi-index \(\nu\),
\[
 \sum_j\psi_j(x)^2=1,
 \qquad
 \operatorname{supp}(\psi_j)\subseteq
 \{x:\lVert x-\ell j\rVert_\infty\le\ell\},
 \qquad
 \lVert D^\nu\psi_j\rVert_\infty\le C_\nu\ell^{-|\nu|},          \tag{20}
\]
and at most \(3^d\) functions are active at any point.

Let \((\vartheta_j)_{j\in J_\ell}\) be independent Rademacher signs and define
\[
 F_\vartheta(x)=k_{x_0,h}(x)\sum_j\vartheta_j\psi_j(x),
 \qquad K(x)=K_{x_0,h}(x).                                        \tag{21}
\]
Independence of the signs and (20) imply, with \(B=3^{d/2}\),
\[
 \mathbb E_\vartheta F_\vartheta(x)=0,
 \qquad
 \mathbb E_\vartheta F_\vartheta(x)^2=K(x),
 \qquad
 |F_\vartheta(x)|\le B.                                          \tag{22}
\]
The product rule, (20), and \(\ell\le h\) show, for every fixed \(s>0\),
\[
 \lVert F_\vartheta\rVert_{\mathcal H_d^s}\le C_s\ell^{-s},
 \qquad
 \lVert K\rVert_{\mathcal H_d^s}\le C_sh^{-s}.                  \tag{23}
\]
Here the constants are uniform in \(\vartheta\), \(x_0\), \(h\), and \(\ell\).  To verify the fractional part explicitly, put \(m=\lceil s\rceil-1\).  An order-\(m\) derivative at scale \(r\) is bounded by \(Cr^{-m}\), while the mean-value theorem bounds its increment by \(Cr^{-m-1}\lVert x-y\rVert_\infty\).  Splitting according as \(\lVert x-y\rVert_\infty\le r\) or \(>r\) gives
\[
 |D^\nu f(x)-D^\nu f(y)|
 \le Cr^{-s}\lVert x-y\rVert_\infty^{s-m},
 \qquad |\nu|=m,
\]
including the integral case \(s-m=1\).  This proves (23) under the frozen definition of \(\mathcal H_d^s(L)\).

For \(\varepsilon\in\{-1,1\}\), define
\[
\begin{aligned}
 e_\vartheta&=p+aF_\vartheta,\\
 \mu_{0,\varepsilon,\vartheta}&=\frac12+\varepsilon bF_\vartheta
       +\frac{\varepsilon ab}{1-p}K,\\
 \tau_\varepsilon&=-\frac{\varepsilon ab}{p(1-p)}K,\\
 \mu_{1,\varepsilon,\vartheta}&=\frac12+\varepsilon bF_\vartheta
       -\frac{\varepsilon ab}{p}K.                                \tag{24}
\end{aligned}
\]
Choose deterministic scales and amplitudes
\[
 \ell=c_\ell n^{-\eta/S},
 \qquad h=\ell^{S/\gamma},
 \qquad a=c_a\ell^\alpha,
 \qquad b=c_b\ell^\beta,                                         \tag{25}
\]
where \(0<c_\ell\le1\) and \(c_a,c_b>0\) will be fixed below.  Since \(S\le S_\star=d\gamma/(2\gamma+d)<\gamma\), (25) gives \(0<\ell\le h\le1\).  Equations (23)--(25) give
\[
 a\ell^{-\alpha}=c_a,
 \qquad b\ell^{-\beta}=c_b,
 \qquad ab h^{-\gamma}=c_ac_b,
 \qquad ab h^{-\beta}
 =c_ac_b\ell^{S(1-\beta/\gamma)}\le c_ac_b.                       \tag{26}
\]
Starting from the constant functions \(4p=3/2\) and \(1/2\), choose \(c_a,c_b\) sufficiently small, depending only on \((d,\alpha,\beta,\gamma,L)\).  The derivative and seminorm estimates (23), the identities (26), the bound (22), the positive denominators \(p=3/8\) and \(1-p=5/8\), and \(L\ge4\) then prove
\[
 4e_\vartheta\in\mathcal H_d^\alpha(L),
 \quad 1\le4e_\vartheta\le2,
 \quad \mu_{0,\varepsilon,\vartheta}\in\mathcal H_d^\beta(L),
 \quad \tau_\varepsilon\in\mathcal H_d^\gamma(L),
 \quad \frac18\le\mu_{a,\varepsilon,\vartheta}\le\frac78.     \tag{27}
\]
Indeed, the two nonconstant terms in \(\mu_0\) are controlled at order \(\beta\) by \(b\ell^{-\beta}\) and \(ab h^{-\beta}\), respectively; the analogous statement holds for \(\mu_1\), and the order-\(\gamma\) norm of \(\tau_\varepsilon\) is controlled by \(ab h^{-\gamma}\).  Thus no smoothness of the marginal outcome regression is imposed or used.

For each \((\varepsilon,\vartheta)\), draw \(X\) exactly uniformly on \(D\), draw \(A\mid X=x\) as \(\operatorname{Bernoulli}(e_\vartheta(x))\), draw \(Y(0)\) and \(Y(1)\) conditionally independently as Bernoulli variables with the respective means in (24), independently of \(A\) given \(X\), and set \(Y=AY(1)+(1-A)Y(0)\).  This construction satisfies consistency and conditional exchangeability, and its observed response is Bernoulli with regression \(\mu_{a,\varepsilon,\vartheta}\).  Therefore (27), together with the exact uniform design, proves that every constructed law is in \(\mathcal P(d,\alpha,\beta,\gamma,L)\).  Let \(\Pi_\varepsilon\) be uniform over the finite set of sign vectors.  Since \(K(x_0)=1\), the target is constant under each prior and
\[
 |\tau_+(x_0)-\tau_-(x_0)|=\frac{2ab}{p(1-p)}.                    \tag{28}
\]

We now bound the mixtures in the actual fixed-\(n\) product experiment.  At a fixed \(x\), replace \((a,\varepsilon b)\) in (24) by real variables \((s,t)\), and abbreviate \(F=F_\vartheta(x)\).  Direct multiplication in the four cells \((A,Y)=(1,1),(1,0),(0,1),(0,0)\) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
q_{11}&=p/2+sF/2+ptF+st(F^2-K)-s^2tKF/p,\\
q_{10}&=p/2+sF/2-ptF-st(F^2-K)+s^2tKF/p,\\
q_{01}&=(1-p)/2-sF/2+(1-p)tF-st(F^2-K)-s^2tKF/(1-p),\\
q_{00}&=(1-p)/2-sF/2-(1-p)tF+st(F^2-K)+s^2tKF/(1-p).              \tag{29}
\end{aligned}
\]
Taking the sign expectation in (29) and using (22) makes every term involving \(F\) vanish and makes \(\mathbb E_\vartheta(F^2-K)=0\).  Hence the one-observation sign average is
\[
 q_0=(p/2,p/2,(1-p)/2,(1-p)/2)
\]
for both signs of \(t\).  Thus every singleton component agrees exactly; in particular there is no macro-scale or singleton leakage.

After decreasing \(c_a,c_b\), if necessary, all ratios \(q_z/q_{0,z}\) lie in \([1/2,3/2]\) for \(|s|\le a\) and \(|t|\le b\), and their first \(s\)-derivatives, first \(t\)-derivatives, and mixed derivatives are bounded by a constant depending only on the fixed parameters.  For fixed locations \(x_1,\ldots,x_r\), define the conditional mixture likelihood ratio
\[
 M_r(s,t;z_{1:r})=
 \mathbb E_\vartheta\prod_{i=1}^r
 \frac{q_{z_i}(s,t;x_i)}{q_{0,z_i}}.
\]
The product rule has \(r\) terms with both derivatives on one factor and \(r(r-1)\) terms with the derivatives on distinct factors.  Since each undifferentiated factor is at most \(3/2\),
\[
 |\partial_s\partial_tM_r(s,t;z_{1:r})|
 \le Cr^2(3/2)^r.                                                  \tag{30}
\]
At \(s=0\), the change of variables \(\vartheta\mapsto-\vartheta\) gives \(M_r(0,b)=M_r(0,-b)\).  Therefore two applications of the fundamental theorem of calculus yield
\[
 |M_r(a,b)-M_r(a,-b)|
 \le \int_0^a\int_{-b}^{b}
 |\partial_s\partial_tM_r(u,t)|\,dt\,du
 \le Ca b r^2(3/2)^r.
\]
Moreover, every product inside the expectation defining \(M_r\) is at least \(2^{-r}\), so \(M_r\ge2^{-r}\).  With \(Q_{r,+}\) and \(Q_{r,-}\) denoting the two conditional component mixtures, the identity \((\sqrt u-\sqrt v)^2=(u-v)^2/(\sqrt u+\sqrt v)^2\), followed by the preceding two bounds and summation against the baseline mass \(q_0^{\otimes r}\), gives
\[
 H^2(Q_{r,+},Q_{r,-})
 \le Ca^2b^2r^4(9/2)^r,
 \qquad r\ge2.                                                     \tag{31}
\]

Condition on \(X_{1:n}\).  Discard from the graph observations outside the support of \(k_{x_0,h}\), since their conditional laws are exactly baseline under both priors.  Connect two retained observations when \(\lVert X_i-X_j\rVert_\infty\le2\ell\).  If two observations use a common sign coordinate, (20) forces their distance to be at most \(2\ell\); hence distinct graph components use disjoint sign coordinates.  Independence of the Rademacher coordinates therefore factors each conditional mixture over the graph components.  Multiplication of Hellinger affinities and \(1-\prod_j u_j\le\sum_j(1-u_j)\), for \(u_j\in[0,1]\), show that the conditional squared Hellinger distance is at most the sum of the component bounds (31).

Let \(N_r\) be the number of size-\(r\) components.  Every connected labeled \(r\)-set contains a spanning tree.  The Pr\"ufer-code deletion procedure gives exactly \(r^{r-2}\) labeled trees.  For a fixed tree, integrate first its root, which must lie in a set of volume at most \((2h)^d\), and then each child, which must lie in an \(L^\infty\)-ball of volume at most \((4\ell)^d\) about its parent.  The uniform-design assumption thus gives
\[
 \mathbb E N_r
 \le {n\choose r}r^{r-2}(2h)^d(4\ell)^{d(r-1)}.                   \tag{32}
\]
Using \({n\choose r}\le n^r/r!\), \(r!\ge(r/e)^r\), and (31)--(32), the sum over \(r\ge2\) is bounded by a constant times
\[
 a^2b^2h^d\sum_{r\ge2}r^2(C_0n\ell^d)^{r-1}n.
\]
If \(C_0n\ell^d\le1/2\), this geometric-polynomial series is bounded by its first-order scale, and hence
\[
 \mathbb E_XH^2\{\mathsf M_+(\cdot\mid X_{1:n}),
                         \mathsf M_-(\cdot\mid X_{1:n})\}
 \le Cn^2h^d\ell^da^2b^2.                                       \tag{33}
\]
The two mixtures have the same uniform \(X_{1:n}\)-marginal.  Integrating their conditional Hellinger affinities against this common marginal shows that the left side of (33) equals the unconditional squared Hellinger distance between the genuine fixed-\(n\) mixtures.  Neither an occupancy event nor Poissonization is used.

It remains to check the tuning conditions.  Because all denominators are positive,
\[
 1-\frac{d\eta}{S}\le0
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 S\le\frac{d\gamma}{2\gamma+d}=S_\star.                         \tag{34}
\]
Thus \(n\ell^d\le c_\ell^d\); at equality it is exactly \(c_\ell^d\), so choosing \(c_\ell\) sufficiently small proves the component-series condition without a logarithmic loss.  Furthermore,
\[
 n^2h^d\ell^da^2b^2
 =c_a^2c_b^2n^2\ell^{2S+d+Sd/\gamma}
 =C(c_a,c_b,c_\ell),                                               \tag{35}
\]
because the definition of \(\eta\) gives \(\eta(2+d/S+d/\gamma)=2\).  Here \(C(c_a,c_b,c_\ell)\) contains the positive power \(c_\ell^{2S+d+Sd/\gamma}\), so a further decrease of \(c_\ell\) makes (33) at most \(1/4\).  Finally, (28) and (25) give
\[
 |\tau_+(x_0)-\tau_-(x_0)|
 =\frac{2c_ac_bc_\ell^S}{p(1-p)}n^{-\eta}
 =c\rho_n.                                                        \tag{36}
\]
All chosen constants are positive and depend only on \((d,\alpha,\beta,\gamma,L)\), uniformly in \(x_0\).  Equations (27), (31), (33), and (36) prove, respectively, same-class support, the asserted component estimate, the genuine fixed-product affinity bound, and target separation.

The upper lemma supplies one finite Borel estimator, namely the branch-defined and clipped \(\widehat\tau_n(x_0)\).  Therefore the definition of minimax risk and \(\mathrm{lem:closed\mbox{-}regime\mbox{-}fixed\mbox{-}point\mbox{-}upper}\) give
\[
 R_n\le\sup_{P\in\mathcal P(d,\alpha,\beta,\gamma,L)}
 \mathbb E_{P_O^{\otimes n}}|\widehat\tau_n(x_0)-\tau_P(x_0)|
 \le C\rho_n.                                                     \tag{37}
\]

For the converse, take the two finite priors from \(\mathrm{lem:closed\mbox{-}regime\mbox{-}fixed\mbox{-}point\mbox{-}component\mbox{-}mixtures}\), let \(\mathsf M_+\) and \(\mathsf M_-\) be their genuine fixed-\(n\) observed-data mixtures, and let their constant target values be \(\theta_+\) and \(\theta_-\).  Put \(\Delta=|\theta_+-\theta_-|\ge c_0\rho_n\).  If \(m_+\) and \(m_-\) are densities relative to a common dominating measure, Cauchy--Schwarz gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \lVert\mathsf M_+-\mathsf M_-\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}
 &=\frac12\int|\sqrt{m_+}-\sqrt{m_-}|(\sqrt{m_+}+\sqrt{m_-})\\
 &\le\frac12H(\mathsf M_+,\mathsf M_-)
 \left\{\int(\sqrt{m_+}+\sqrt{m_-})^2\right\}^{1/2}\\
 &\le H(\mathsf M_+,\mathsf M_-)\le\frac12.                     \tag{38}
\end{aligned}
\]
The last inequality uses the component-mixture theorem's bound \(H^2\le1/4\).

Fix an arbitrary Borel estimator \(T\), and define a test \(\varphi\in\{+,-\}\) by selecting the target value nearer to \(T\), with deterministic tie breaking.  An error under sign \(\varepsilon\) implies \(|T-\theta_\varepsilon|\ge\Delta/2\).  Since each prior is supported on \(\mathcal P(d,\alpha,\beta,\gamma,L)\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \sup_{P\in\mathcal P(d,\alpha,\beta,\gamma,L)}
 \mathbb E_{P_O^{\otimes n}}|T-\tau_P(x_0)|
 &\ge\frac12\sum_{\varepsilon\in\{+,-\}}
       \int\mathbb E_{P_O^{\otimes n}}|T-\theta_\varepsilon|\,
       d\Pi_\varepsilon(P)\\
 &\ge\frac\Delta4\{\mathsf M_+(\varphi=-)+\mathsf M_-(\varphi=+)\}\\
 &\ge\frac\Delta4
       \{1-\lVert\mathsf M_+-\mathsf M_-\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}\}\\
 &\ge\frac{c_0}{8}\rho_n.                                       \tag{39}
\end{aligned}
\]
The penultimate inequality is the variational definition of total variation applied to the acceptance set.  Taking the infimum over all Borel \(T\) proves the lower bound.  The priors are supported on the exact-uniform, full-support Bernoulli class, so (39) concerns precisely the stipulated fixed-\(n\) product experiment.  If a broader model contains this exact class and uses the same point target \(\tau_P(x_0)\), its supremum risk is at least the supremum over this subclass, so the lower bound transfers upward.  Equation (37) was proved only for the exact-uniform class and makes no upper-bound claim for a broader model.

Combining (37)--(39) yields \(R_n\asymp\rho_n\), with constants uniform in the fixed known \(x_0\).  At \(S=S_\star\), direct substitution gives
\[
 \eta=
 \left(1+\frac d{2\gamma}+\frac{2\gamma+d}{2\gamma}\right)^{-1}
 =\frac\gamma{2\gamma+d},
\]
so the same-class oracle power \(n^{-\gamma/(2\gamma+d)}\) is attained without a logarithmic multiplier.  If \(S<S_\star\), the same algebra gives \(\eta<\gamma/(2\gamma+d)\), and hence
\[
 \frac{R_n}{n^{-\gamma/(2\gamma+d)}}
 \asymp n^{\gamma/(2\gamma+d)-\eta}\longrightarrow\infty.
\]
Thus, within the stipulated closed regime, oracle order is attained exactly at the elbow.

By \(\mathrm{def:rate}\),
\[
 \eta=\left(1+\frac{d}{2\gamma}+\frac{d}{2S}\right)^{-1}.
\]
The declared definition of \(\rho_n^{\mathrm{or}}\) gives
\[
 \rho_n^{\mathrm{or}}=n^{-q_{\mathrm{or}}},
 \qquad
 q_{\mathrm{or}}:=\frac{\gamma}{2\gamma+d}
 =\left(2+\frac d\gamma\right)^{-1}.
\]
All of \(d\), \(S\), and \(\gamma\) are strictly positive by their declared spaces.  Hence both denominators above are positive, and cross-multiplication preserves inequality directions.  Consequently,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \eta<q_{\mathrm{or}}
 &\Longleftrightarrow
 1+\frac{d}{2\gamma}+\frac{d}{2S}>2+\frac d\gamma\\
 &\Longleftrightarrow \frac{d}{2S}>1+\frac{d}{2\gamma}\\
 &\Longleftrightarrow d\gamma>S(2\gamma+d)\\
 &\Longleftrightarrow
 S<\frac{d\gamma}{2\gamma+d}=S_\star.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus, in the strict regime \(S<S_\star\), the quantity \(\delta:=q_{\mathrm{or}}-\eta\) is positive.  By \(\mathrm{thm:sharp\mbox{-}exact\mbox{-}uniform\mbox{-}rate}\), there are constants \(0<c\le C<\infty\), independent of \(n\), such that
\[
 c n^{-\eta}\le R_n\le C n^{-\eta},
 \qquad n\ge2.
\]
Since \(\rho_n^{\mathrm{or}}=n^{-q_{\mathrm{or}}}>0\), division gives
\[
 c n^{q_{\mathrm{or}}-\eta}
 \le\frac{R_n}{\rho_n^{\mathrm{or}}}
 \le C n^{q_{\mathrm{or}}-\eta},
\]
or equivalently
\[
 \frac{R_n}{\rho_n^{\mathrm{or}}}\asymp n^\delta.
\]
Because \(\delta>0\), \(n^\delta\to\infty\), so
\[
 \frac{R_n}{\rho_n^{\mathrm{or}}}\longrightarrow\infty.
\]
Thus no parameter tuple in the strict below-elbow regime attains the same-class oracle order.

At the boundary allowed by \(\mathrm{ass:below\mbox{-}elbow}\), namely \(S=S_\star\), all the preceding equivalences hold with equality and
\[
 \eta=q_{\mathrm{or}}=\frac{\gamma}{2\gamma+d}.
\]
The sharp-rate theorem then yields
\[
 c n^{-\gamma/(2\gamma+d)}
 \le R_n\le
 C n^{-\gamma/(2\gamma+d)}.
\]
Both sides are pure powers of \(n\), so no logarithmic multiplier occurs.  Hence the same-class oracle benchmark is attained exactly at the elbow and is unattainable throughout the strict below-elbow regime.

proposed.comparator_claim: Theorem 1 gives a lower bound on a broader bounded-density pointwise CATE class, while Theorem 2 gives an upper bound under additional design and nuisance-estimation conditions; the displayed lower hard laws use separated local support.
Theorem 2.1 bounds the affinity of two convex mixtures of product measures under a measurable partition and coordinate-local perturbations.
Theorems 3--5 establish matched local and global conditional-variance rates under random design using local U-statistics and coupled lower laws.
Theorem 3 and Corollary 4 give local-polynomial R-learner upper rates with deterministic smoothness-dependent tuning under known-density conditions.
The paper proves a quasi-oracle error bound for an R-learner under sufficient nuisance accuracy rather than a rough-nuisance pointwise minimax converse.

prose_updates.related_work: KennedyBalakrishnanRobinsWasserman2024MinimaxCATE is the closest comparator: its lower theorem covers a broader bounded-density class and its upper theorem requires additional design and nuisance-estimation conditions, whereas the present result closes the fixed-\(n\) converse and matching upper bound on the strict exact-uniform bounded-overlap Bernoulli/interiority subclass. The lower converse therefore transfers upward by subclass inclusion to any broader model that contains this subclass and uses the same point target; the exact-uniform upper proof does not transfer in that direction and is not claimed there. RobinsTchetgenLiVanderVaart2009SemiparametricMinimax supplies the product-mixture perspective, but the shared smooth frames here require random overlap-component factorization rather than a deterministic coordinate-local partition. ShenGaoWittenHan2020Variance is a random-design nonlinear-functional analogue for repeated local occupancy. Kennedy2023DRCATE and NieWager2021RLearner provide oracle-facing upper comparisons, while RobinsLiTchetgenVanderVaart2008HOIF motivates the finite projection correction. LiuMukherjeeRobinsTchetgen2021Adaptive studies adaptive nonlinear-functional estimation, whereas the present estimator uses known smoothness. LeeOkuiWhang2017CATEBands studies uniform CATE confidence bands, whereas this note proves pointwise mean-risk only. AtheyWager2021PolicyLearning studies policy-value and regret learning rather than pointwise CATE minimax precision. ChernozhukovWuthrichZhu2021Conformal studies conformal counterfactual and synthetic-control inference rather than this estimand or guarantee. WagerAthey2018CausalForests is an application-facing consumer: this is a precision benchmark for \(\texttt{causal\_forest}\) and R-learner workflows, not a claim that existing forests attain the bound.
